definition: All the living organisms in an area and the non-living (abiotic) conditions they interact with.
All the populations of different species living in the same area at the same time.
All the individuals of the same species living in the same area at the same time.
The place where an organism lives, providing food, shelter and the conditions it needs to survive.
A non-living factor that affects the distribution and abundance of organisms, e.g. temperature, light, pH, water availability.
A living factor that affects organisms in an ecosystem, e.g. predators, prey, disease, competition.
The way in which organisms in a community depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and other needs.
An organism (usually a plant) that produces its own food by photosynthesis — the first organism in a food chain.
An organism that obtains energy by eating other organisms.
An animal that hunts and kills other animals (prey) for food.
An animal that is hunted and eaten by a predator.
A sequence showing the transfer of energy from one organism to the next, starting with a producer.
A network of interconnected food chains showing the feeding relationships in an ecosystem.
The position an organism occupies in a food chain — producers are level 1, primary consumers level 2, etc.
The total mass of living material in an organism or at a trophic level, usually measured as dry mass.
A diagram showing the relative biomass at each trophic level — always wider at the base (producers).
An organism (bacteria or fungi) that breaks down dead organic material, releasing nutrients back into the soil.
The process by which carbon is recycled through the environment via photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion.
The process by which nitrogen is recycled through the environment, involving nitrogen-fixing bacteria, decomposers and denitrifying bacteria.
Bacteria that convert atmospheric nitrogen gas into ammonia or nitrates that plants can use.
Bacteria that convert nitrates in the soil back into nitrogen gas, removing nitrogen from the ecosystem.
The breakdown of dead organic material by decomposers (bacteria and fungi), recycling nutrients back into the soil.
The continuous movement of water through the environment via evaporation, condensation, precipitation and transpiration.
The variety of different species of organisms on Earth, or in a particular ecosystem.
The permanent disappearance of all members of a species from Earth.
The large-scale cutting down of forests, which reduces biodiversity, increases CO₂ and reduces carbon storage.
The process where excess fertilisers run into water, causing rapid algal growth, reduced light, death of plants, decomposition by bacteria and depletion of oxygen.
The build-up of toxic substances (e.g. pesticides) in organisms, becoming more concentrated at higher trophic levels.
The increase in the average temperature of the Earth's surface due to the enhanced greenhouse effect.
A gas that absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation, trapping heat in the atmosphere. Examples include CO₂, methane and water vapour.
The natural process by which greenhouse gases trap heat from the Sun in the Earth's atmosphere, warming the planet.
The total amount of greenhouse gases produced by an individual, organisation or activity, usually measured in CO₂ equivalent.
A species whose presence or absence indicates the health of an ecosystem — e.g. lichens indicate clean air, mayfly larvae indicate clean water.
The protection and management of ecosystems and species to maintain biodiversity.
A square frame used to sample the number and distribution of organisms in an area.
A line along which organisms are sampled at regular intervals to show how their distribution changes across an area.
The process of studying a representative part of an ecosystem to estimate the total population or distribution of species.
The struggle between organisms for the same limited resources, such as food, water, light or space.
